vignette: Mr. Raj Singh is a 79-year-old South Asian man who served in the military and now works part-time at a local warehouse. His divorce several years ago marked the end of a tumultuous relationship that left him feeling emotionally drained. Mr. Singh has recently sought help for overwhelming symptoms following his traumatic experiences during combat. Mr. Singh vividly remembers the day he witnessed intense fighting, seeing comrades fall and feeling the constant fear of not surviving each moment. The sound of gunfire still echoes in his mind, even now decades later. He reports frequent nightmares where he relives those moments, waking up drenched in sweat with a racing heart. These intrusive memories have been relentless, making it difficult for him to sleep at night. At work, the loud noises from machinery and the constant movement can sometimes trigger flashbacks. Recently, while stacking boxes on high shelves, a sudden bang from another part of the warehouse sent him into a panic. The memory of gunfire flooded back, causing him to freeze in fear and shake uncontrollably. He quickly left his shift early that day, feeling too shaken to continue. Mr. Singh has come to believe that he is not safe anywhere, that danger lurks around every corner. This belief has made it hard for him to engage with life as he once did. He avoids crowds and loud environments, limiting his social interactions outside of work. He had thought about joining a community group or attending events but the fear of being in an environment where unexpected sounds could trigger another episode kept him from doing so. The impact on his daily functioning has been significant. His sleep is disrupted almost nightly by nightmares and he often finds himself lying awake, consumed by thoughts of that day long ago. At work, he avoids certain areas where machinery noise is louder, which has made completing some tasks more challenging. He worries about making mistakes or being unable to perform well due to his heightened state of anxiety. Mr. Singh's relationships have also been affected. His son tries to visit regularly but often hears Mr. Singh's distressing memories over dinner. Despite his son's efforts to be supportive, Mr. Singh often pushes him away out of frustration with his own inability to cope. He is certain that sharing these experiences will only add to the burden on his family. What frightened Mr. Singh most was not just the traumatic event itself but how it continues to haunt him in everyday life. He had hoped that time would ease the pain, yet he has found no relief. It became clear to him that without help, he might never regain control over his life. The decision to seek therapy came after a particularly severe episode at work where he felt completely overwhelmed and unable to function. Mr. Singh is hopeful that with support, he can learn to manage these intrusive memories and fears, reclaiming some semblance of normalcy in his daily life.
